So the hinterland won out. Makes a Difference WHICH Hinter land It Is But when the Poles wanted Danzig, the reasoning shifted. The whole valley of the Vistula is Polish; the city of Danzig is German. We were told that Danzig must not go to Poland because the population of Danzig is German, although the population of the hinter land is Polish. But when it comes to Fiume, Fiume must not be given to the Italians be cause although the population of the city is Italian, the hinterland is Jugo-Slav.

items.excerpt: In a little different way we grown-ups during the last few years have been doing a merry-go-round marathon. of our own. We have been chasing the high cost of living round and round in a circle. And the faster we have galloped the more speed it has seemed to acquire. Many have believed that high wages would solve the problem, but as most of us have begun to realize, they won’t. The reason is that every time you raise wages you increase the cost of production, and by increasing the cost of production you increase the price of goods. It doesn’t do any of us any [good] to get more money for our work if we have to turn around and spend more money for our living expense[s].

items.excerpt: The high cost of living is an issue felt in every home in the United States. Step by step the cost of liv ing has been increasing since the ar mistice, even as it increased before the armistice, and there is today no [m]ore promise of relief than there was six months ago. The increasing cos[t] of living has been in effect a reduction of the purchasing power of a dollar fully one-half. Those who earn today the same [nu]mber of dollars they earned in 1913 and in the early months of 1914 are getting in real wages one-half the amount they earned then because of this reduction in the buying power of the dollar. To earn the same amount in real wages that they earned in 1913 [th]e workers must earn t[w]ice the num ber of dollars, and there are thousands upon thousands who have not been able to advance their wages to any appreciable extent.

The increasing cos[t] of living has been in effect a reduction of the purchasing power of a dollar fully one-half. Those who can af[f]ord to hold their grain long enough may b[e] able to come out on top. But, many who cou[l]d have sold at a good [fi]gure a short time ago, are worried now be cause they did not sell. Much of the troub[l]e can be laid to the foolish ad vice of Dr. Ladd, who advised farmers to hold their grain for a certain price. Hundreds did as he suggest[e]d. Then a million-bushel crop from Canada was dropped on our markets, and re ports of an over-supply in South America sent the prices tumbling. Prof. Ladd has caused the farmers of this state to lose "millions [of] dollars" by loosely giving advice without knowing what he was talking about.

items.excerpt: East St. Louis women do not seem to care for their newly won right to vote for all offices. at least they showed little interest in the first opportunity to register which was given under the law last Saturday. Out of a total of 13,000 registered less than 35 per cent are women. This lack of interest on the part of the women was unexpected. It was thought that a larger per cent age of the city’s women would enroll themselves, especially because of universal suffrage and the additional fact that this is the presidential year. Four years ago East St. Louis had a registration of 25,[0]00 for the presi dential election and, of this number over 8,000 were women. If the proportionate registration of women is not increased on October 12, the next and last. registration day, this city will not have more than about 6,000 women eligible to vote on No vember 2 [next].

items.excerpt: REGISTRATION OF WOMEN VOTERS Registration Books Open Sept 30th and Close Oct. 23rd. All White Women Over 21 [Years] Old Eligible [for] Registration. Editor Post-Dispatch Just a word about registration of voters. Whatever may have been the individual wishes of any person in this county, we are now confronted with the fact that women are entitled to vote on the same footing as are the men. The registration books will open in every precinct on Thursday, September 30th and close on Saturday, October 23rd, and during that time we should use every means to have the women of this county register for the election to be held the first Tuesday in the coming November. I want to see all the white women in the county register between September 30 and Oc tober 23rd and to that end the men should lend every assist ance. I trust the precinct com mitteemen will see that the women voters as well as the men are duly registered.

By so doing they express their gratitude for their enfranchisement and make manifest their quick response to their new responsibilities. But best reason of all it is probable that Missis[s]ippi women will yet have a right to have "their prayers counted o[n] election day.” Though many able attorneys have held that Mississippi women cannot qualify to vote this year on account of the four months registration law, others equally eminent maintain that they can vote in November provided they register immediately. Former Justice, Chas. E. Hughes, counsel for the National Suffrage Association, has looked into the Mississippi laws at the request of Mrs. Catt, and is of the opinion that Mississippi women are entitled to vote provided they register immediately after the promulgation of the suffrage amendment.

items.excerpt: CHICAGO, Sept. 24.—Big breaks in the price of wheat took place to day as result of agitation for a general cut in food costs. The smash of values in wheat amounte[d] to as much as 12 and thre[e] quarters cents per bushel and the market closed in a semi-demoralized condi tion. December deliveries at $2.25 to $2.25 1-2 and March at $2.15 to $2.16. Heretofore wh[e]at has been advan cing despit[e] [t]he setbacks in the price of other grains. The chief reason ascribed was huge sales for export to Europe. Today the stimulus of export business appeared to have lost influence and especially near the end of the day wheat tumble[d] wildly downward. In sympathy with the weakness of wheat other grain markets gave way and both corn and oats fell to lowest yet for 1920 crop.

items.excerpt: Mrs. E. A. Yost. Washington. D. C.. representing the Women's Christian Temperance [U]nion. said strict enforcement was a "moral duty" and asked a plank pledging "honest" enforcement. Enforcement Plank Asked. Frank M. Silsey, representing the Presbyterian national general assembly also asked for an enforcement plank and protested against any weakening of the Volstead act. Former Representative Richmond Pearson Hobson of Alabama, submitted a plank expressing party pride in the national prohibition amendment. Char les J. Hall, representing temperance or ganizations. said prohibitionists had been "handed a gold brick at Chicago." Henry Clay Needham of the national prohibition party asked if the Demo crats wanted "these millions of votes." referring to the dry sentiment in the country.

Kiggins, chief prohibition enforcement officer of central and southern Illinois.

items.excerpt: Women have been granted the ballot in Illinois. This naturally includes colored women since Illinois is above the Mason-Dixon line. We would imagine that all of the colored women in this favored land would take advantage of this splendid opportunity to become a part of the great system of government which heretofore they have been denied. The registration booths were very much devoid of colored women on registration night but to the contrary, the cabarets and the dance halls were filled to the overflow. ‘‘Oh judgment, thou hast flown to brutish beasts.”

items.excerpt: JACKSONVILLE, Fla., Oct. 9.—The first arrest since negro women began flooding registration offices to take advantage of woman suffrage took place in Jacksonville yesterday when Juanita Allen, colored, was taken into custody upon the complaint of Frank M. Ironmonger, Supervisor of Registration. The charge placed against the woman was perjury. Registration officials said 500 warrants had been sworn out for negro women, who, it is charged, have made fal[s]e affidavits as to their age or residence in the county and state, and that they will be served on Election Day. According to Mr. [I]ronmonger, the Allen woman swore that she was twenty-one years old. Under close questioning she admitted that she was born April 12, 1902, and later said she was only nineteen years old. When asked her reason for trying to register when under age, the defendant replied that a number of negroes had threatened to kill her unless she registered.

items.excerpt: East St. Louis women do not seem to care for their newly won right to vote for all offices. at least they showed little interest in the first opportunity to register which was given under the law last Saturday. Out of a total of 13,000 registered less than 35 per cent are women. This lack of interest on the part of the women was unexpected. It was thought that a larger per cent age of the city’s women would enroll themselves, especially because of universal suffrage and the additional fact that this is the presidential year. Four years ago East St. Louis had a registration of 25,[0]00 for the presi dential election and, of this number over 8,000 were women. If the proportionate registration of women is not increased on October 12, the next and last. registration day, this city will not have more than about 6,000 women eligible to vote on No vember 2 [next].

items.excerpt: In a little different way we grown-ups during the last few years have been doing a merry-go-round marathon. of our own. We have been chasing the high cost of living round and round in a circle. And the faster we have galloped the more speed it has seemed to acquire. Many have believed that high wages would solve the problem, but as most of us have begun to realize, they won’t. The reason is that every time you raise wages you increase the cost of production, and by increasing the cost of production you increase the price of goods. It doesn’t do any of us any [good] to get more money for our work if we have to turn around and spend more money for our living expense[s].

Step by step the cost of liv ing has been increasing since the ar mistice, even as it increased before the armistice, and there is today no [m]ore promise of relief than there was six months ago. The increasing cos[t] of living has been in effect a reduction of the purchasing power of a dollar fully one-half. Those who earn today the same [nu]mber of dollars they earned in 1913 and in the early months of 1914 are getting in real wages one-half the amount they earned then because of this reduction in the buying power of the dollar. To earn the same amount in real wages that they earned in 1913 [th]e workers must earn t[w]ice the num ber of dollars, and there are thousands upon thousands who have not been able to advance their wages to any appreciable extent.

items.excerpt: East St. Louis women do not seem to care for their newly won right to vote for all offices. at least they showed little interest in the first opportunity to register which was given under the law last Saturday. Out of a total of 13,000 registered less than 35 per cent are women. This lack of interest on the part of the women was unexpected. It was thought that a larger per cent age of the city’s women would enroll themselves, especially because of universal suffrage and the additional fact that this is the presidential year. Four years ago East St. Louis had a registration of 25,[0]00 for the presi dential election and, of this number over 8,000 were women. If the proportionate registration of women is not increased on October 12, the next and last. registration day, this city will not have more than about 6,000 women eligible to vote on No vember 2 [next].

items.excerpt: AGENTS KEEP UP DRIVE TO CLEAN OUT ‘GOOSE HILL’ Prohibition enforcement officers yesterday afternoon continued their drive to clean up "Goose Hill," a foreign settlement in the North End. Three arrests were made and two barrels of mash and several bottles of illicit liquor confiscated. The men taken into custody are: Mike Kalish, owner of a saloon at Third street and Exchange avenue; John Riecon, owner of a saloon at 413 Winstanley avenue, and Walter Gregorich, who occupies rooms above the establishment Kalish conducts.

items.excerpt: The high cost of living is an issue felt in every home in the United States. Step by step the cost of liv ing has been increasing since the ar mistice, even as it increased before the armistice, and there is today no [m]ore promise of relief than there was six months ago. The increasing cos[t] of living has been in effect a reduction of the purchasing power of a dollar fully one-half. Those who earn today the same [nu]mber of dollars they earned in 1913 and in the early months of 1914 are getting in real wages one-half the amount they earned then because of this reduction in the buying power of the dollar. To earn the same amount in real wages that they earned in 1913 [th]e workers must earn t[w]ice the num ber of dollars, and there are thousands upon thousands who have not been able to advance their wages to any appreciable extent.

items.excerpt: LAW OF STATE PROVIDES FOR WOMEN VOTING The last Mississippi legislature made provision for allowing women to vote when the suffrage amendment was ratified, the qualifications being [t]he same as for male voters. The laws passed by the legislature on this subject follow: Chapter 153, House Bill No. 576. An act providing for the voting by women in primary elections. Section 1. Be it enacted by the legislature of the State of Mississippi That women may vote in all primary elections, under the same conditions, qualifications, requirement[s] and penalties that govern t[h]e vot[ing] of men in such elections. The payment of poll taxes shall hereafter be required of females the same as is now required by law of male citizen.

items.excerpt: It is the duty of Mississippi women to register at once. By so doing they express their gratitude for their enfranchisement and make manifest their quick response to their new responsibilities. But best reason of all it is probable that Missis[s]ippi women will yet have a right to have "their prayers counted o[n] election day.” Though many able attorneys have held that Mississippi women cannot qualify to vote this year on account of the four months registration law, others equally eminent maintain that they can vote in November provided they register immediately. Former Justice, Chas. E. Hughes, counsel for the National Suffrage Association, has looked into the Mississippi laws at the request of Mrs. Catt, and is of the opinion that Mississippi women are entitled to vote provided they register immediately after the promulgation of the suffrage amendment.

items.excerpt: REGISTRATION OF WOMEN VOTERS Registration Books Open Sept 30th and Close Oct. 23rd. All White Women Over 21 [Years] Old Eligible [for] Registration. Editor Post-Dispatch Just a word about registration of voters. Whatever may have been the individual wishes of any person in this county, we are now confronted with the fact that women are entitled to vote on the same footing as are the men. The registration books will open in every precinct on Thursday, September 30th and close on Saturday, October 23rd, and during that time we should use every means to have the women of this county register for the election to be held the first Tuesday in the coming November. I want to see all the white women in the county register between September 30 and Oc tober 23rd and to that end the men should lend every assist ance. I trust the precinct com mitteemen will see that the women voters as well as the men are duly registered.

items.excerpt: REGISTRATION OF WOMEN VOTERS Registration Books Open Sept 30th and Close Oct. 23rd. All White Women Over 21 [Years] Old Eligible [for] Registration. Editor Post-Dispatch Just a word about registration of voters. Whatever may have been the individual wishes of any person in this county, we are now confronted with the fact that women are entitled to vote on the same footing as are the men. The registration books will open in every precinct on Thursday, September 30th and close on Saturday, October 23rd, and during that time we should use every means to have the women of this county register for the election to be held the first Tuesday in the coming November. I want to see all the white women in the county register between September 30 and Oc tober 23rd and to that end the men should lend every assist ance. I trust the precinct com mitteemen will see that the women voters as well as the men are duly registered.

items.excerpt: LAW OF STATE PROVIDES FOR WOMEN VOTING The last Mississippi legislature made provision for allowing women to vote when the suffrage amendment was ratified, the qualifications being [t]he same as for male voters. The laws passed by the legislature on this subject follow: Chapter 153, House Bill No. 576. An act providing for the voting by women in primary elections. Section 1. Be it enacted by the legislature of the State of Mississippi That women may vote in all primary elections, under the same conditions, qualifications, requirement[s] and penalties that govern t[h]e vot[ing] of men in such elections. The payment of poll taxes shall hereafter be required of females the same as is now required by law of male citizen.

items.excerpt: Proposition No. 2 (the Harris State Prohibition Enforcement Act) does not represent true California sentiment. The measure it self is the product of the last Legislature, which absolutely misrep resented the majority wish of the people of this State on the question of prohibition. In 1914. 191[6] and 191[8] California voted down prohibition by very decisive majorities. Within sixt[y] days after the people had rejected the third attempt of the prohibitionists, a Legislature dominated by radical “drys" performed the startling feat of placing this State in the prohibition column by ratifying the Eighteenth Amendment an[d] passing the Harris Act in California by way of enforcement.

items.excerpt: AGENTS KEEP UP DRIVE TO CLEAN OUT ‘GOOSE HILL’ Prohibition enforcement officers yesterday afternoon continued their drive to clean up "Goose Hill," a foreign settlement in the North End. Three arrests were made and two barrels of mash and several bottles of illicit liquor confiscated. The men taken into custody are: Mike Kalish, owner of a saloon at Third street and Exchange avenue; John Riecon, owner of a saloon at 413 Winstanley avenue, and Walter Gregorich, who occupies rooms above the establishment Kalish conducts.

items.excerpt: In a little different way we grown-ups during the last few years have been doing a merry-go-round marathon. of our own. We have been chasing the high cost of living round and round in a circle. And the faster we have galloped the more speed it has seemed to acquire. items.excerpt: We hear a great deal about the woman vote as a distinct force in elections. It is our experience that nothing is changed by it. The women vote very much the same as the men do on candidates and public policies. For instance if there is one social and political question on which it is assured that the women vote differently from the men it is the question of prohibition. The general assumption is that the women's vote was almost solid against the saloons and for prohibition. Yet when Chicago voted on this question a majority of the women's votes were against prohibition as was also the case with the men's votes. The women vote against prohibition showed a slightly lower majority than was the case with the men, but still not a great deal of difference. Illinois is the only state where the vote of the men and women is counted separately, so such comparisons can not be made in other states.

The measure it self is the product of the last Legislature, which absolutely misrep resented the majority wish of the people of this State on the question of prohibition. In 1914. 191[6] and 191[8] California voted down prohibition by very decisive majorities. Within sixt[y] days after the people had rejected the third attempt of the prohibitionists, a Legislature dominated by radical “drys" performed the startling feat of placing this State in the prohibition column by ratifying the Eighteenth Amendment an[d] passing the Harris Act in California by way of enforcement.
